_note: Every fact below comes from the source URL in the record (mostly NASA NSSDCA catalogue pages). Coordinates are planetocentric degrees, east longitude positive (-180 to 180); NSSDCA values given in 0-360 E or W were converted. null = not found in a verified source. Full source list: docs/research-sources.md

objects.name: Surveyor 3
objects.status: Still on the Moon (some parts returned to Earth)
objects.purpose: A robotic lander sent to prove a spacecraft could land softly on the Moon and to study the surface, to prepare for crewed Apollo landings.
objects.story: Its engines kept firing, so Surveyor 3 touched down three times before settling inside a small crater on 20 April 1967. It worked until after sunset on 3 May 1967. Two and a half years later, on 19 November 1969, Apollo 12 landed about 180 m away. Astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over and removed parts, including its TV camera, and brought them back to Earth.
objects.science: Surveyor 3 sent back 6,326 TV pictures and dug trenches up to 18 cm deep to test the lunar soil. The parts carried home by Apollo 12 let scientists study hardware that had spent years on the Moon.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 12 photo AS12-48-7134 (Alan Bean at Surveyor 3, Apollo 12 lunar module behind)

objects.name: Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector
objects.purpose: A panel of 100 special mirrors (corner cubes) that bounce laser light straight back to where it came from, so scientists on Earth can measure the exact distance to the Moon.
objects.story: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin set it up near their lander Eagle during the first Moon walk in July 1969. Unlike the other experiments, it needs no power at all, which is why it still works more than 50 years later.
objects.science: By timing laser pulses that bounce off reflectors like this one, scientists found that the Moon is slowly moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm every year.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 11 photo AS11-37-5551 (laser reflector in front, seismometer behind)

objects.name: Apollo 11 Passive Seismometer (EASEP)
objects.status: Stopped working in 1969; still on the Moon
objects.purpose: A solar-powered station to measure moonquakes and learn about the Moon's crust and interior. It also carried a detector to measure how much dust settled on it.
objects.story: Buzz Aldrin set it up about 17 m south of the lander. It was switched on from Earth on 21 July 1969 while the astronauts were still outside. It kept working even though it got 30 °C hotter than planned. On 27 August 1969 it stopped accepting commands from Earth, and the experiment ended.
objects.science: It was designed to measure seismic activity and the physical properties of the lunar crust and interior. It could only work in daylight because it ran on solar panels.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 11 photo AS11-40-5942 (Buzz Aldrin carrying the experiments)

objects.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
objects.purpose: A car carried folded up on the lunar module, so astronauts could travel much farther from their lander than on foot.
objects.story: Apollo 15 landed on 30 July 1971 at the foot of the Apennine mountains. David Scott and James Irwin used the rover to explore areas up to 5 km from the lander. It was the first time a vehicle like this had been used on the Moon, and it worked very well. Only the top part of the lander flew back, so the rover stayed behind.
objects.science: With the rover's help, the crew covered 27.9 km on three moonwalks and collected 77.31 kg of rocks and soil for scientists on Earth.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 15 photo AS15-86-11603 (James Irwin at the rover)

objects.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP)
objects.status: Switched off in 1977; still on the Moon
objects.purpose: A science station left on the Moon to keep sending measurements to Earth after the astronauts went home. It was powered by a SNAP-27 radioisotope generator, not solar panels.
objects.story: Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, the crew of the last Apollo landing, set it up during their first moonwalk. It was switched on on 12 December 1972. On 30 September 1977 it was shut down along with all the other Apollo science stations.
objects.science: It sent data from the Moon for almost five years. On the same mission the crew set off explosive packages for a seismic experiment, and Schmitt, the first scientist to walk on the Moon, discovered a patch of orange soil.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JSC – Apollo 17 photo AS17-147-22548 (ALSEP in the background)

objects.name: Viking 1 Lander
objects.purpose: Study the biology, chemistry, weather, quakes, magnetism and surface of Mars from the ground.
objects.story: Viking 1 touched down in Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976 and started sending its first surface picture just 25 seconds after landing. Its seismometer never unlocked and a stuck pin on its sampler arm took 5 days to shake loose, but the lander kept working until 13 November 1982, when contact was lost.
objects.science: It took the first photograph ever taken on the surface of Mars and studied martian soil, weather and air for more than six years.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JPL – PIA00381, the first photograph taken on the surface of Mars

objects.name: Sojourner Rover
objects.purpose: A small six-wheeled rover (63 cm long, 28 cm high) to show that landing on and driving across Mars could be done at low cost.
objects.story: Mars Pathfinder landed on 4 July 1997 inside giant airbags, bouncing at least 15 times before it stopped. Sojourner rolled down a ramp onto Mars on 6 July. The lander and rover worked until 27 September 1997, when communications were lost for unknown reasons.
objects.science: Sojourner tested rocks and soil in Ares Vallis, one of the largest outflow channels on Mars. It was carved by a huge ancient flood, possibly as much water as all five Great Lakes.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JPL – PIA04318, Sojourner near the "Rock Garden"

objects.name: Spirit Rover
objects.purpose: A robot geologist sent to search rocks and soils for clues about past water and whether life could ever have existed on Mars.
objects.story: Spirit landed in Gusev Crater on 4 January 2004. It kept exploring even after one of its six wheels stopped working. On 23 April 2009 it broke through a thin crust into soft sand and got stuck. Its solar panels could not get enough sunlight to survive the winter, and its last transmission came on 22 March 2010.
objects.science: Spirit travelled 7.73 km over 6 years and 2 months. It explored Gusev Crater, which may once have been filled with water.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JPL – PIA16442, Spirit self-portrait from the McMurdo panorama (2006)

objects.name: Opportunity Rover
objects.purpose: Spirit's twin: a robot geologist looking for clues about past water and whether life could ever have existed on Mars.
objects.story: Opportunity arrived on 25 January 2004 and rolled to a stop inside a crater only 20 m wide. It kept exploring for more than 14 years, until its final message to Earth on 10 June 2018.
objects.science: It explored Terra Meridiani, nicknamed the "Hematite Site" because it contains hematite, an iron-rich mineral that usually forms in water.

objects.name: Phoenix Mars Lander
objects.purpose: Dig into the icy ground of the Mars arctic to study water, ice and the polar climate, and whether the area could ever have supported life.
objects.story: Phoenix landed on 25 May 2008 in the far north of Mars, where the ground holds a lot of ice. As the martian summer ended there was less sunlight for its solar panels, and it sent its last signal on 2 November 2008.
objects.science: On 31 July 2008 NASA announced that Phoenix had confirmed water on Mars in a soil sample, and the mission was extended.
objects.imageCredit: NASA/JPL – PIA10691, Phoenix footpad on Mars (May 2008)

objects.name: InSight Lander
objects.purpose: Listen for marsquakes and measure heat and the planet's wobble to find out what Mars is like inside: its core, mantle and crust.
objects.story: InSight landed in western Elysium Planitia on 26 November 2018. Over four years, dust slowly covered its solar panels until they could not make enough power. NASA declared the mission over on 21 December 2022.
objects.science: Its seismometer recorded 1,319 marsquakes, including one of about magnitude 5 on 4 May 2022, and helped reveal the structure of Mars' interior.
